Spothole - Pothole AI

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Using Autonomous Vehicle Technology to help fix a very South African problem

Unique Selling Point:
Realising that South Africa is a far way away from self-driving vehicles, a young inventor from CT, Audrey Mnisi, has come up with an innovative way to use Self-driving technology and AI to help address the current pothole pandemic in South Africa.

Summary:
It’s a little box — called Amehlo — about the size of an external hard drive that can be fitted into any vehicle. Together with a small sensor/camera, it is able to analyse road infrastructure anomalies in real time, which means that users can instantly see the condition of a road, potholes, and even the tiniest of cracks. This invention, repurposing existing technology could be a game-changer when it comes to inspecting our road infrastructure and reporting issues to authorities, or even the public. Amehlo gathers, aggregates, and analyses environmental data using Synthetic Aperture Radar, Depth Optical Sensor, Active Radar, and LiDAR.

With this device, there is no need to “report a pothole” — the system will do it automatically and based on accumulative information, can give the end user a clear picture of the all over state of any road.

So I propose that we pit our Pothole Hunters (Claire and Trusty Assistant) against Amehlo… and see what happens!
Can also obviously speak to experts to explore the possible uses of the technology/device


Further information:
The dream is to have some sort of interface with a GPS map system, like Waze or Google maps, that will guide drivers, not just based on traffic and congestion, but also road quality… Ideal for Insurance companies who would like to minimise claims from pothole-vehicle damage…

But the information is not limited to potholes… it can also report on road markings (paint condition etc), traffic signs, as well as the electricity and plumbing network next to a road.

All this is brought to South Africa by a young, dynamic inventor and founder of sensorit — a tech startup in cape Town

Travel to CT
Car hire

Press Release:


There’s a pothole pandemic in South Africa and motorists have had enough. Now, by repurposing existing self-driving technology and artificial intelligence, a young inventor has found an advanced solution to tackling our pothole dilemma.
Poetically named Amehlo, which means eyes, it’s a little device that used modern GPS and other technology to identify and map potholes and other areas of crumbling road infrastructure – even to the point of “seeing” them before they develop. That data provides a “real-time” picture of the state of various roads. It allows drivers to plan their journeys to avoid the worst-affected roads and lets administrators know what requires fixing... and how soon.  

Producer:
Stenette Grosskopf | Presenter: Claire Mawisa 

Script:


POTHOLE AI FINAL SCRIPT
Sci fi music
A long time… a not-so-long time ago, right here in South Africa…
UPSOUND
Look how deep that is!

Jeez
V/O
In April, Trusty Assistant and I drove over 2500kms in search of the worst roads in South Africa –
UPSOUND
I’m in Koster, another small town in South Africa and the roads are shocking. Sad to say I’m not surprised…
UPSOUND
1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6… 10 potholes in this just small space.

That’s about 2 metres.

What?
V/O
… from North West to Mpumalanga and the Free State….
UPSOUND
There’s all the ones we’re going through and then there’s all the ones we’re not going through.

I’m trying to miss them but you have to choose the lesser of the pothole.
V/O
We were shocked…


UPSOUND
Free State roads will traumatise me for the rest of my life. I was depleted after the Free State leg of this journey…
Link
With any service delivery failure story we do viewers are very quick to point out that – in the Western Cape – things are different…

So, it wouldn’t be a “scientific study” if we didn’t come and see for ourselves. I’ve got one problem, though… Trusty Assistant is in bed with a very bad case of Man Flu… so I’m going to need to find a suitable alternative…
Drone shot of car – CT


V/O
My search for the ultimate “Trusty Assistant-replacement” takes me to the University of Cape Town… to find Amehlo…
V/O

No that’s not him…

That’s…it…… a pothole spotting super assistant that is said to change the way we monitor road infrastructure.


V/O
And it was born right here in this unassuming lab, where Aubrey Mnisi and his team have been experimenting with innovative ways of using cutting-edge technology to help address a very every-day South African problem…
Aubrey Mnisi
Amehlo is an intelligent vision system that we’ve developed, primarily to aid, not just government, but anyone that’s interested in infrastructure…
V/O
Amehlo – which means eyes, or vision – uses Artificial Intelligence (AI) to detect, measure and compute an array of road infrastructure flaws…
Aubrey Mnisi
Claire: So if you had to explain it for someone who thinks, listen, these engineering guys are very complicated… How would you explain it? How would you explain it to…

Aubrey: My mother…

Claire: to your mother.

Aubrey: Absolutely. The same way we’re asked by the government to take out our phone as a motorist or as a pedestrian, when we see an infrastructure flaw, take a picture with the available apps… So Amehlo is an automatic version of that…


V/O
Amehlo uses the same technology that runs a self-driving car to “read” the road surface… recording things like displaced manhole covers, potholes and even the smallest of cracks… And all that information is instantly available to users.
V/O
It’s one of a series of revolutionary innovations from Aubrey, who calls himself a Solutionist… with roots right here in Khayelitsha…
Aubrey Mnisi
Aubrey: Here, this is my home… this is where I grew up as a kid…

I understood my situation, right, because I understood we’re poor. I wasn’t pretending to myself. You know that’s what we often do. People are unable to save themselves out of poverty because they’re not able to look at it for what it is.
V/O
Aubrey studied finance, but the idea of being tied to a 9-to-5 job did not appeal to him, so he set his sights on something greater…
Claire & Aubrey
Aubrey: I didn’t come this far just to come this far, s o for me that’s why I am working crazy hours for example, because there is no plan B. I am the plan, you know. It kinda has to work.

Claire: There’s no other way. It’s plan A or Plan A.

Aubrey: Or plan A.1


V/O
This plan led Aubrey to an ambitious collaboration with UCT.


Aubrey Mnisi
When we started with the project we actually wanted to build a self-driving car. But then after spending some time I actually realised the end product in Africa is not a self-driving car through autonomous systems… at least for the next 10 to 15 years. The end product is actually leveraging on the technology that makes up a self-driving car to create contextualised applications. Like, Amehlo, for example.


V/O
During our previous pothole story, I found out, first-hand, that counting and recording road surface flaws is no easy task… even with a Trusty Assistant by my side.

We drove thousands of kilometres to record the state of some of our roads, but often, we simply couldn't keep up…
Trusty
For this I’ve just written A LOT in allcaps… very scientific!
Claire & Aubrey
Aubrey, are you trying to tell me that Amehlo is better?

Aubrey: Absolutely, absolutely. It’s far better.

Claire: Wow. His feelings are hurt, I just want you to know.

Aubrey: No, we love him, but this is more automatic, that has a higher data integrity than a human, that would for instance have to sit in a room, zooming into a picture for them to understand the actual size of that given pothole. So all of that can happen automatically now…


V/O
But it’s about more than just spotting potholes… Amehlo is gathering information. The dream is to have thousands of Amehlos in cars all over the country, building a detailed map of our roads… laying the foundation for an autonomous driving future … right here in South Africa…
Aubrey Mnisi
Remember, you can take a self-driving car that has been taught in America to come drive here – it won’t know what to do. But then if you give it, or feed it data that is contextualised and local it will then know what to do,

Claire: So Elon is going to call you…

Aubrey: I’m expecting a call…
V/O
Amehlo can be fitted to any vehicle. Using one of their earlier prototype models, they prepare to take us for a quick demonstration.


UPSOUND - You can’t film the inside.
That’s the IP.
V/O
It uses a sim card for connectivity and a small camera placed in the car’s grill gives it eyes!

UPSOUND
This is it, Guys!
V/O
Ironically, Aubrey doesn’t like driving… which is probably why he’s so keen on the concept of autonomous vehicles.
Aubrey & Claire
Claire: So me asking you to drive was actually not a good thing?

Aubrey: Um, I’m not opposed to driving, it’s just not my favourite task.
V/O
To find potholes in Cape Town, we head to Langa…
Claire & Aubrey
Ooh, so let me tell you when we decided to do this story we asked all of our viewers to send us your worst roads in SOuth Africa. You know, Capetonians and Westerncapers - your people… they were so smug… They were like, what is a pothole, who is a pothole… describe it for us because it’s such a rare thing for us.

Aubrey: Absolutely, I mean in the city of course there isn’t so much potholes because it’s well-maintained, but you will see as we’re driving into the township now there’s more potholes than anything…
V/O
Langa lies just west of the city, but in reality it’s a different world…


UPSOUND

Aubrey: Oh no there is no road there…

Claire: No. The road ends. I don’t even think you can call that a pothole. It’s over…


V/O
And while Aubrey tries to navigate the narrow roads, Amehlo quietly gets on with its business, counting and measuring the infrastructure anomalies… and this data can be instantly accessed by any road management agency, streamlining the maintenance process.


Aubrey
If you pick up a crack it would probably cost you R700 per square metre. But if you wait a little bit longer, it will cost you twice as much… R1 400…
Explain the current uses
Insurance companies could also use the information to supply drivers with better options – A GPS map that not only gives you the fastest route, but the best drivable road - potentially cutting down on pothole-related claims.
Claire & Aubrey
Claire: It sounds like, rolled out on a large scale, it can actually make a large impact…

Aubrey: Absolutely

Claire:.. In us maintaining our infrastructure…
V/O
For Aubrey, Amehlo is not the end of the road. His PLAN A is a highway to putting South Africa at the forefront of cutting edge technology…
Claire & Aubrey
Is 10-year old Aybrey proud of you?

Aubrey: Very, I mean I didn’t even know I’d be doing half the things I’m doing right now. What makes everything what it is, is the sense of belief that I have. If you think you can and you can’t, you’re right… on both accounts, you know. So I think that’s what people need to understand. If you come from here you’ve got nothing to lose…

Claire: You’ve got nothing to lose!

Aubrey: So, why don’t you just leverage on that and use that as a fuel to somewhat go for your wildest dreams or ideas.

Claire: Is that the benefit of being the underdog?

Abrey: Absolutely!








PROMO 1 11”
From humble beginnings …to putting South Africa on the global technology map… Aubrey Mnisi is a man with big aspirations…

UPSOUND AUBREY: If you come from here you have nothing to lose…


PROMO 2 21”
It’s a mini computer with eyes, counting and measuring potholes, even spotting the smallest of cracks…

UPSOUND: You drive around as we’re driving now and the systems will be gathering detections, and issues in the infrastructure and all that information is logged into our platform.

Using cutting edge technology to help fix a very South African problem…
PROMO 3 21”
Using self-driving technology, this little box is about to change the way we assess road infrastructure…

Amehlo is an intelligent vision system that can with great degree of accuracy pick up potholes…

A giant leap towards preparing the country for autonomous vehicles….

UPSOUND: So El n is going to call you?
I’m expecting the call.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Using Autonomous Vehicle Technology to help fix a very South African problem
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Realising that South Africa is a far way away from self-driving vehicles, a young inventor from CT, Audrey Mnisi, has come up with an innovative way to use Self-driving technology and AI to help address the current pothole pandemic in South Africa.
metadata.Summary: It’s a little box — called Amehlo — about the size of an external hard drive that can be fitted into any vehicle. Together with a small sensor/camera, it is able to analyse road infrastructure anomalies in real time, which means that users can instantly see the condition of a road, potholes, and even the tiniest of cracks. This invention, repurposing existing technology could be a game-changer when it comes to inspecting our road infrastructure and reporting issues to authorities, or even the public. Amehlo gathers, aggregates, and analyses environmental data using Synthetic Aperture Radar, Depth Optical Sensor, Active Radar, and LiDAR. With this device, there is no need to “report a pothole” — the system will do it automatically and based on accumulative information, can give the end user a clear picture of the all over state of any road. So I propose that we pit our Pothole Hunters (Claire and Trusty Assistant) against Amehlo… and see what happens! Can also obviously speak to experts to explore the possible uses of the technology/device
metadata.Further information: The dream is to have some sort of interface with a GPS map system, like Waze or Google maps, that will guide drivers, not just based on traffic and congestion, but also road quality… Ideal for Insurance companies who would like to minimise claims from pothole-vehicle damage… But the information is not limited to potholes… it can also report on road markings (paint condition etc), traffic signs, as well as the electricity and plumbing network next to a road. All this is brought to South Africa by a young, dynamic inventor and founder of sensorit — a tech startup in cape Town
